clue.text: Sir is almost beastly about antioxidants?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the word, so its final letter is dropped
about can mean around or in a different order, so the gathered letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its last letter lopped off

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that a knight is being nearly beastly about antioxidant supplements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' looks like an adjective about Sir; it is fodder, trimmed by 'almost' and then shuffled with SIR IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Antioxidants are added to foods and plastics to keep them from degrading, so they serve as one example of stabilising additives, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Everyone tour operator's taking to Turin initially

indicators.note: initially points at the opening letter of each of the words before it
taking means the company swallows the other letters, holding them within itself

blocks.note: TUI is a big European package-holiday company
first letters of to and Turin

explanation.surface: A holiday firm takes a whole party of travellers to Turin.
explanation.walkthrough: TUI is a well-known British and German package-holiday company; the word 'taking' looks like transporting, but it means holding inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti is the Italian musical direction telling all players or singers to perform together, so it means all of them.

clue.text: Heavy material in what could be Shirley Temple's biggest feature?

definitions.text: what could be Shirley Temple's biggest feature?

blocks.note: first meaning: weighty stuff such as gravel or iron carried low in a vessel for stability

blocks.clueFragment: what could be Shirley Temple's biggest feature?
blocks.note: second meaning, cryptic: her signature song is about the Good Ship Lollipop, and the bulkiest thing aboard a ship is the weight in its hold

explanation.surface: A film buff wonders which heavyweight element made Shirley Temple's biggest movie.
explanation.walkthrough: Shirley Temple, the 1930s child star, is best remembered for singing On the Good Ship Lollipop; a ship's heaviest feature is what sits low in its hull.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships carry dense stuff such as gravel, iron or water low down to keep them stable, and that weighty cargo is exactly heavy material.

clue.text: Somewhere to go with family by chance

blocks.note: a loo is a toilet, the place you go when you need to go
joins the two pieces
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: Looking for a place to visit with the family, leaving it all to luck.
explanation.walkthrough: Loo is everyday British for toilet, and 'somewhere to go' is the euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: A look-in is an informal word for an opportunity to take part or succeed, as in not getting a look-in.

clue.text: Batter Ben Stokes snubbed is South African

definitions.note: the clue uses an adjective as a noun: the answer is an animal of South Africa

indicators.note: snubbed suggests cut short, like a snub nose, so the name loses its last letter
to batter is to beat out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: the name with its final letter dropped

explanation.surface: The batsman Ben Stokes, ignored by selectors, turns out to be South African.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Stokes is England's Test cricket captain and a batter, which makes 'Batter' read as a noun rather than the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The steenbok is a small antelope native to southern Africa, so it is a South African creature.

clue.text: Break sculpture, say and kick off once more

blocks.note: a break is a rest
sculpture is an example of art; 'say' flags the example

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a statue and then starts the match again.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick off is to begin a football match, and doing that again after a stoppage is starting anew.

clue.text: One's message can be driven home

definitions.text: One's message can be driven home

blocks.clueFragment: One's message can be driven home
blocks.note: surface reading: someone's point can be forcefully made, hammered home
setter's reading: a slogan on the back of a car is literally carried home as the car is driven

explanation.walkthrough: 'Driven home' is the idiom for making a point stick, but here it is a literal journey by car.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan label stuck on the rear of a vehicle displays a message that travels wherever the car is driven.

clue.text: Nottingham side convinced Saints must withdraw as predicted

indicators.note: to withdraw is to pull out, so those letters leave the string

blocks.note: Nottingham Forest is the city's football club
to be sold on something is to be convinced
S is the abbreviation for saint, so two saints are two S's

explanation.surface: A football report: Nottingham Forest are convinced that Southampton, the Saints, will pull out, just as forecast.
explanation.walkthrough: Saints is the nickname of Southampton FC, which adds to the football picture; here it means two S's, removed from FORESTSOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: To foretell is to prophesy, so something foretold has been forecast in advance.

clue.text: Standing next to Mark Gatiss for the finale in Calvin Klein briefs & a Rolex?!

indicators.note: next to says one piece is placed directly beside the following one
the finale is the end, so only the closing letter of the name is wanted

blocks.note: standing is social rank
a mark or sign
last letter of Gatiss

explanation.surface: The actor Mark Gatiss appears at the end of a show wearing only designer underpants and a Rolex.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Gatiss is an English actor and writer (Sherlock, The League of Gentlemen); 'Mark' must be split off from him as a separate word.
explanation.definitionFit: Designer underwear and luxury watches are worn partly to show off wealth, examples of possessions that signal rank.

clue.text: Before taking seconds to guess one's star sign cleverly

indicators.note: seconds asks for the letter in second place of each word that follows

blocks.note: second letters of guess, one's, star, sign and cleverly

explanation.surface: Before having another go, someone tries to work out a person's star sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like time or a second helping; it means the second letter of each of the last five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words can mean up to the time that, as in wait until dark or not before dark.

clue.text: Go too far up waterslide by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says to go by how the word is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: up as in finished: time is up, time is over
a waterslide is a chute, which is said like a word for firing

explanation.surface: Someone goes too far up a waterslide.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot is to pass beyond a target or stopping point, literally or by exceeding a limit.

clue.text: Distress of soldier wanting electronic one that's charged

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is missing from the word before it

blocks.note: a private is the lowest-ranked soldier
E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
I is the Roman numeral one
a device that is charged up and live is on

explanation.surface: A soldier is upset at not having an electronic gadget that's charged up.
explanation.definitionFit: Privation is hardship from lacking necessities, a state of want and suffering close to distress.

clue.text: Expert caddies putt regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: On the golf course, skilful caddies sink putts as a matter of routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert caddies' reads as a phrase; 'Expert' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Adept works as both adjective and noun meaning a highly skilled person or someone very proficient.

clue.text: Management removed first and second TV directors?

indicators.note: first and second gives the order in which the two words are placed

blocks.note: remote means distant, far removed
controls as in those in charge, the management

explanation.surface: Television bosses were dismissed, with management sacked first and the directors second.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the words out of order: 'removed' goes first and 'Management' second.
explanation.definitionFit: Handheld zappers let you change channel and volume from the sofa, so they direct the TV, playfully put.

clue.text: Mould of a metal dish

indicators.note: to mould is to shape or form, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cast or mould made out of a metal dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mould' reads as a noun, a casting form; it is the verb telling you to reshape the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Minced beef baked in a loaf shape is a familiar main course, so it is one example of a dish.

clue.text: See 14
Insensibility leads to orchestra's bassoonist trashing violin

indicators.note: leads are the front runners, so the opening letters of the next words are taken
trashing something wrecks it, so the instrument's letters are scrambled

blocks.note: first letters of orchestra's and bassoonist
taken as written, then scrambled

explanation.surface: An orchestra's bassoonist wrecks a violin, which leads to a stupor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads to' looks like 'results in'; it means take the leading letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Oblivion is the state of being unconscious or unaware of surroundings, which is insensibility.

clue.text: Strangely they all hated cover of biggest song

indicators.note: a cover wraps the outside, so only the outer letters of the next word are kept
strangely means in an odd way, so all the following letters are put in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written
first and last letters of biggest

explanation.surface: Oddly, everyone loathed the cover version of the biggest hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover' suggests a cover version of a song, matching the surface; it means just the outside letters of 'biggest'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the 1957 hit by Buddy Holly and the Crickets, so the answer is the title of a song.

clue.text: Record including name put on silver ring in the distant past

indicators.note: including means holding inside, so the record wraps round the next piece
put on means placed next to, so the pieces are joined in sequence

blocks.note: a log is a written record
N is the abbreviation for name
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A record with a name engraved on a silver ring from long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a time far back, ages since, an adverb matching the adverbial phrase.

clue.text: See 18
Hospital doctor stopping you having a little something containing water

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so one piece sits inside another
a little of the word means only a small bit of it, its first letter

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
taken as written
Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
first letter of something

explanation.surface: A hospital doctor stops you having a snack that contains water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little something' sounds like a snack, but it asks only for the opening letter of 'something'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydrous is a chemistry term for compounds or minerals that hold water in their structure.

clue.text: Traditions of America for example brought up by son

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means raised from the bottom, so the abbreviation reads upwards

blocks.note: the United States of America
e.g. abbreviates for example
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: American customs, for instance, raised by a son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' just places the son beside the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Usages are established customs or habitual practices, so the plural is equivalent to traditions.

clue.text: Schoolboy oddly ignored new feature of digital clock display

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are ignored, so only the even ones are kept

blocks.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of schoolboy
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A schoolboy strangely overlooks a new feature on a digital clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' sounds like 'strangely', but it means the letters in odd positions.
explanation.definitionFit: A digital clock shows two stacked dots between hours and minutes, the punctuation mark separating them.

clue.text: Perhaps sewing mailbags as a result of this crime?

blocks.clueFragment: Perhaps sewing mailbags as a result of this crime?
blocks.note: surface reading: a criminal ends up doing menial work as punishment for some offence
setter's reading: sewing mailbags was traditional prison labour, work done while locked up, so it describes the crime and also the work it leads to

explanation.walkthrough: Prisoners in British jails were once set to sew mailbags; the answer means both a crime committed with help from within and work done in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a robbery or fraud carried out by, or with help from, someone working at the target.

clue.text: Energy drink for one

blocks.note: first meaning: informal for power, fuel or electricity
second meaning: an example of a beverage, such as orange

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a can of energy drink for one person; 'for one' signals an example instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses the word for electric power or petrol, and it is also the liquid squeezed from fruit, a beverage.

clue.text: Coming from chap devouring sandwiches

indicators.note: sandwiches means enclosing between two slices, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: devouring is eating greedily
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A man comes away from wolfing down sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' reads as food being devoured; it is the verb meaning to enclose.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to issue or originate from a source, so emanating means proceeding from.

clue.text: Gold that is left in bay window

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
i.e. abbreviates that is
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Gold left lying in a bay window.
explanation.definitionFit: An oriel is a projecting upper-storey window bulging out from a wall, a kind of bay.

clue.text: Music equipment's somehow messy in studio after cutting two singles

indicators.note: cutting means taking out, so some letters are removed before the shuffle
somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written
a single is one, I in Roman numerals, so two singles are two I's

explanation.surface: The music kit in the studio has somehow got messy after two singles were recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting two singles' suggests recording records; it means removing two I's from the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Amplifiers, speakers and decks together make up a setup for playing music loud, which is music equipment.
